conversation.content:
Good morning. I’m so glad you’re here. My name is Dr. Ramirez, and I’m the perinatal mental-health clinician who works with new moms. I’m going to spend a few quiet minutes with you to do something called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—most people just say “the EPDS.” It’s a short set of 10 questions that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling in the past week since your baby arrived. There are no right or wrong answers; we simply want to make sure we’re catching anything that might be weighing on you so we can offer the best support. Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me someone is in immediate danger. We’ll go gently, one question at a time, and you can pause or ask for clarification whenever you need.

Shall we begin?

First, I’d love to know: in the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

I can laugh sometimes—like if my partner makes a joke or the baby makes a silly face—but it doesn’t come as easily as it used to. I’ll chuckle, but it feels kind of flat, like the happiness doesn’t last.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah, I can still laugh, just... not as much or as hard as before. It feels like I have to remind myself to find things funny, and even when I do laugh, it fades pretty fast.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I do look forward to some things—like taking the baby for a short walk or having my morning coffee—but the excitement isn’t as strong as it used to be. It’s more like “that’ll be nice” instead of really counting down the hours like I did before she was born.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

A couple of times this week, yeah. Like when she wouldn’t settle at 3 a.m., I kept thinking maybe I’m not feeding her right or I missed some cue, even though everyone says it’s normal. I know rationally it’s not really my fault, but the thought still pops in.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes. Like yesterday I suddenly worried her breathing sounded different, even though I’d just checked on her and she was fine. I calmed myself pretty quickly, but it came out of nowhere and made my chest feel tight for a minute or two.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
Not really panicky—more just that quick jolt of worry I mentioned. It passes fast once I take a breath or two, so I wouldn’t call it scared, just a little on-edge out of the blue.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days, yeah. Like when the laundry piles up or she’s fussy during her whole nap window, I feel a bit swamped. I usually manage to get through it, but it feels harder than it should—like I’m wading through molasses just to finish the basics.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not really. I’ve had a little trouble drifting off a couple of nights because my mind keeps running through the next day’s tasks, but once I’m out I sleep fine. The sadness doesn’t keep me awake—just the usual new-mom racing thoughts.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… I do feel kind of down some parts of the day, usually when I’m alone feeding her. It’s not all day, and I’m not crying constantly, but there’s this low mood that lingers even when nothing bad happened.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

I’ve cried a couple of times this week—once when she wouldn’t latch and once when I dropped a plate and it shattered. It wasn’t all day or anything, just those moments when everything felt a bit too much and the tears came for a minute or two.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I’ve felt tired or overwhelmed, but I haven’t had any thoughts like that.

You've shared that while you can still laugh and look forward to small pleasures, the joy feels muted and fleeting; you often blame yourself when your baby won't settle, notice sudden worry about her breathing, feel swamped by ordinary tasks, experience lingering low mood during feeds, and have cried when things feel too much, yet you've had no thoughts of self-harm.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 12, Risk Level: High possibility of depression (concerns include <sym>Patient reports self-blame "a couple of times this week" and describes recurrent intrusive thoughts of fault, matching "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>The patient describes sudden, unexplained worry occurring at least once, matching the frequency of "Yes, sometimes."</sym>, <sym>Describes periodic overwhelm and difficulty coping with daily tasks, matching 'sometimes not coping as well as usual'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports persistent low mood during parts of most days, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS item scoring: Q1=1, Q2=1, Q3=2, Q4=2, Q5=1, Q6=2, Q7=0, Q8=2, Q9=1, Q10=0, summing to 12. A score of 12 places you above the 11-point threshold indicating high likelihood of <med>postpartum depression</med>. Clinically, you endorse five key areas aligned with <med>DSM-5 Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: <sym>depressed mood most of the day</sym>, <sym>markedly diminished interest or pleasure</sym>, <sym>feelings of inappropriate guilt</sym>, <sym>episodes of crying</sym>, and <sym>difficulty coping with daily tasks</sym>. You deny <sym>sleep disruption due to mood</sym> and any <sym>self-harm thoughts</sym>, which are protective. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange an appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> within the next week to review these results and consider further evaluation or treatment
2. Continue sharing your feelings with your partner or support network and accept practical help with baby care, meals, and household tasks to reduce overload
3. Prioritize brief daily walks, balanced nutrition, and rest when the baby sleeps; gentle exercise and sunlight can modestly lift mood
4. Practice 4-7-8 breathing or another brief relaxation technique when sudden <sym>anxiety</sym> or <sym>worry</sym> arises; if chest tightness worsens or panic symptoms develop, seek prompt medical review
5. Schedule a follow-up EPDS or mood check in two weeks to track whether symptoms improve, stay the same, or worsen; bring a written log of mood, crying episodes, and any new <sym>anxiety</sym> spells to that visit
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 12: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: New mother, 1–2 wks postpartum (per self-report)  
Instrument: 10-item EPDS-style clinical interview  
Date: [today]

Symptoms endorsed  
- Persistent low mood (Q8)  
- Marked reduction in pleasure/enthusiasm (Q1, Q2)  
- Episodic tearfulness (Q9)  
- Unwarranted guilt over infant care (Q3)  
- Sudden, brief anxiety episodes with physical tension (Q4, Q5)  
- Feeling “swamped” by routine tasks (Q6)

Severity indicators  
- Symptoms present “some parts of the day,” not continuous  
- No current anhedonia (able to enjoy coffee, walks)  
- No prolonged panic attacks  
- Sleep latency mildly increased by racing thoughts; mood-related insomnia denied (Q7)

Safety screening  
- Denies self-harm ideation (Q10)  
- No suicidal/homicidal content elicited

Risk profile  
- Modest elevation for postpartum depression (core mood + guilt + crying)  
- Mild elevation for postpartum anxiety (spontaneous worry, somatic tension)  
- Protective: intact attachment to infant, social support mentioned, no self-harm thoughts

Recommendation  
Score suggests possible subsyndromal depression / anxiety; consider formal EPDS, PHQ-9/GAD-7, and follow-up within 1–2 weeks to monitor trajectory.
